newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine Congress passes nuclear sell-off law.
newsitem.headline: Argentine Congress passes nuclear sell-off law.

text.p: The Argentine Senate passed a law late Wednesday permitting the privatization of two nuclear power stations and one unfinished plant, and authorizing nuclear waste to be dumped on Argentine soil.

The ruling Peronist Party's majority in the upper house passed the bill, approved by the lower house last August, in five hours' debate with opposition from the Radical Party and provincial parties and some provincial Peronist senators.
Greenpeace staged a small protest outside Congress as the debate took place, calling for the closure of nuclear plants and arguing "there are no economic reasons" for the sell-off.

President Carlos Menem's government has been counting on the long-delayed sale of the Atucha I and Atucha II plants and the unfinished Embalse Rio Tercero plant to raise $200 million already pencilled into the 1997 budget.

Atucha I and Embalse have a joint installed capacity of 1,000 megawatts and generate 15 percent of Argentina's power needs. Atucha II's construction is stalled after 15 years and a condition of the sale is that it be completed in six years.
"Its completion will mean 650 million pesos' investment and five years' work for 5,000 people" said Peronist Sen. Julio San Millan, arguing in favor of the privatization bill.
But rebel Peronist Senator Jose Manuel De la Sota, voting against, said it "offers no safety guarantees when it comes to the closure or dismantling of the plants."
The nuclear sale is one of the last major privatizations left for President Carlos Menem's Peronist government, along with the country's airports and post office.
The law establishes the regulation of the industry by the National Atomic Energy Commission (CNEA) and a six-person watchdog to be appointed by the president and Congress.

It establishes an $80 million obligatory civil accident insurance and gives the CNEA powers to decide the location of nuclear waste dumps. In the case of high-activity waste, it needs the prior approval of relevant provincial parliaments.

Juan Carlos Villalonga, head of Greenpeace's energy campaign in southern part of Latin America, told reporters outside Congress: "The rush and lack of debate with which this whole privatization process is taking place is outrageous."
"It intends to bring new investments to an activity which is not wanted by the Argentine people." (( Stephen Brown, Buenos Aires Newsroom +541 318-0695))
